# In Praise of Moss

There is a patch of moss I think about sometimes, though I have never seen it. It grows on the north side of an imagined stone wall, the kind that runs through old New England woods and marks property lines nobody remembers. The farmers who built those walls are long gone. Their fields have returned to forest. But the moss is still there, doing what it has done for four hundred and seventy million years: waiting, drinking, holding on.

I want to write about moss because it seems to me one of the most underappreciated successes in the history of life, and because thinking about it changes the way I think about almost everything else.

Consider the basic facts. Mosses have no roots, only thin filaments called rhizoids that anchor them but barely absorb anything. They have no vascular system, no internal plumbing to carry water from one part of the plant to another. They have no flowers, no seeds, no fruit. By most of the metrics we use to measure plant sophistication, they are primitive, an early draft that evolution moved beyond. Ferns got vascular tissue. Conifers got seeds. Flowering plants got petals and nectar and the cooperation of bees. Moss, apparently, got left behind.

Except it didn't. There are roughly twelve thousand species of moss alive today, on every continent including Antarctica. They grow on rock faces where nothing else can take hold, on tree bark, on rooftops, in the cracks of city sidewalks. They were among the first plants to colonize land, and they helped make it habitable, breaking down stone into the first soils that later, grander plants would depend on. Everything that came after stood, in some sense, on moss.

What moss has instead of complexity is a kind of radical patience. Most mosses can dry out almost completely, losing nearly all their water, and simply stop. They don't die. They suspend. Their metabolism halts, and they sit there brown and brittle for weeks, months, sometimes years. Then rain comes, and within minutes they unfurl, turn green, and resume photosynthesis as if nothing happened. In 2014, researchers revived moss that had been frozen in Antarctic permafrost for over fifteen hundred years. It grew. Moss that had been dormant since roughly the fall of Rome picked up where it left off.

I find this astonishing, and also instructive. We tend to think of survival as a matter of strength or speed or intelligence: outrunning, outfighting, outthinking. Moss suggests another strategy entirely. Be small. Be flexible. Need little. When conditions turn against you, don't struggle; wait. The storm is not permanent.

There is a garden in Kyoto called Saihō-ji, more commonly known as Kokedera, the Moss Temple. Over a hundred species of moss carpet its grounds in shades of green I'm told are almost impossible to describe: emerald, jade, lime, a green so deep it looks black in the shade. The funny thing is that the moss wasn't originally the point. The garden was designed in the fourteenth century, and for a long time it was a more conventional landscape. The moss arrived later, during periods when the temple lacked the money to maintain the grounds. Neglect let it in. And the monks, rather than fighting it, recognized what had happened and began to tend it.

I love that story because it inverts our usual ideas about cultivation. The most celebrated moss garden in the world exists partly because people stopped trying so hard. The beauty came from attention paid to what grew on its own, not from imposition.

The botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer, in her book *Gathering Moss*, writes about how mosses reward a particular kind of looking. You cannot appreciate them from a distance. From a standing height, a mossy rock is just a green rock. But get down on your knees, bring your face close, and the green resolves into a forest: tiny stems, leaves one cell thick, capsules on slender stalks like miniature lanterns. Water beads on the leaf tips and catches light. Small animals, tardigrades and rotifers and mites, wander through what is to them a vast wilderness. A whole world exists at a scale we routinely step over.

This seems like a lesson worth absorbing. So much of what matters is available only to close attention. We are built, or perhaps trained, to notice the large and the loud: the redwood, not the moss at its base; the headline, not the slow change beneath it. But the moss is doing important work. Peat mosses, the sphagnums, form bogs that cover only about three percent of the Earth's land surface yet store more carbon than all the world's forests combined. Sphagnum can hold up to twenty times its dry weight in water. During the First World War, when cotton was scarce, it was gathered by the ton and used to dress wounds, because it is absorbent and mildly antiseptic. Quiet things holding up the world.

I think there is a temptation, especially now, to measure worth by visibility and growth. Bigger, faster, more. Moss is none of those things. It grows perhaps a centimeter a year, sometimes less. It never towers. It doesn't dominate a landscape so much as soften it, filling the gaps, cushioning the edges, turning hard surfaces into places where other life can begin.

And yet it has outlasted nearly everything. The dinosaurs came and went; the moss remained. Ice ages advanced and retreated; the moss dried out, waited, and returned. Whatever happens next on this planet, I would bet on moss being around for it.

There is something consoling in that. Not every form of flourishing looks like conquest. Some of it looks like a small green thing on the north side of a stone wall, absorbing rain, making a little soil, asking for almost nothing, and persisting across centuries that forgot the people who stacked the stones.

When I think about what it might mean to live well, I don't always think of the redwood. Sometimes I think of the moss: patient, resilient, attentive to small increments of water and light, content to be overlooked, and quietly making the ground a little softer for whatever comes after.
